# Author's note

Back in 2024 I was using beets to catalogue, and eventually normalise, my collection of 90.000+ audio files. Then I hit a wall: beets can't read SACD ISOs. The usual answer is sacd_extract, but driving it from a beets plugin means forking a process for every disc and scraping its text output. Slow and fragile.

So I tried to re-implement the SACD reading in Python, working with ChatGPT. After a few days of banging my head against it I got nowhere. Scarletbook is a niche format, DST decoding is genuinely hard, and I shelved it.

In October 2026 I threw Claude at the problem. It worked. After a few days of building and testing I now have pysacd, a Python module (pip install pysacd) that natively reads the full content of a SACD ISO. Anyone wanting to write a tool for SACD ISOs can now access those contents programmatically from within their Python application: structured objects instead of text to parse, exceptions instead of exit codes. The beets plugin is already published.

This does not replace AutoScript or your PS3 and is not intended to. It works with them exactly like sacd_extract does. Point it at the player's IP and port and get an ISO, DSF or FLAC straight off the disc. The difference is on the client side. Most tools act as a wrapper or front end to sacd_extract - they run it for you and attempt to scrape its output as a text stream. pysacd does the work itself.

pysacd-extract, which is bundled with pysacd, is a proof point that pysacd does what it says on the tin. It acts as a drop-in replacement for sacd_extract: the same options, the same files, byte for byte. If you're happy with your current setup, nothing has to change.

Don't trust me (or the AI), check it. Disc info is identical to sacd_extract on 99 of 99 discs, and 28 of 28 end-to-end output cases are byte-identical. About 6,7 million DST frames (roughly 25 hours of real discs) decode with zero errors. Millions of fuzzing runs and about 95 deliberately broken disc images found and fixed real bugs. CI compares every change against sacd_extract built from upstream source, and you can check it yourself with diff -r.

What it does that sacd_extract doesn't: gapless 24-bit FLAC/WAV, MusicBrainz tags and cover art (plus optional ISRC submission back to MusicBrainz), raw-sector images, and picking a rip back up if the connection to the player drops. Plain DSD discs extract 2,5 to 3,6× faster, and DST discs 2,4 to 2,6× faster. And there's one version: you pip install it, and there's no more "which build of sacd_extract are you running?"

On licensing: sacd_extract's DST decoder derives from the Philips/ISO reference code, which isn't GPL-compatible. That may be part of why we've seen so few GUIs and other tools built on it. pysacd doesn't contain any of that code. It's GPL-2.0-or-later, and its DST decoder builds on FFmpeg's LGPL decoder. The parts FFmpeg was missing were added through a documented clean-room process, and the spec is in the repo so anyone can audit it.

Next up is a full clean-room Rust library, MIT/Apache licensed, written only from a published spec and tested against a public conformance corpus. It'll have a C interface, so you can use it from C, Go, Python or anything else. Open source or commercial, nobody should have to dig through old C code or worry about licensing to write an SACD client again.

After that, a FUSE filesystem. Mount your ISOs and they show up as regular DSF or WAV files, so beets, Plex, Navidrome or any player can read them without extracting anything. Tag edits are stored alongside and never touch the ISO.

Limitations: it's only been tested against a PS3 simulator. If you have a PS3 or player running SACD Ripper or AutoScript, please send me a log. And like sacd_extract, it can't read SACDs from a PC optical drive. You need an ISO or a player.

None of this was practical with just sacd_extract. Better clients for everyone - that's what I'm after.

https://github.com/aclater/pysacd
